nameStory: The Northern Myotis gets its name from its notably long ears that extend well beyond its nose when folded forward - a distinguishing feature among the mouse-eared bats. 'Myotis' comes from Greek meaning 'mouse ear,' referring to the rounded, prominent ears that all bats in this genus share. The 'northern' part of its name reflects its preference for cooler climates in the northern United States and southern Canada.
description: The Northern Myotis is a small, delicate bat about the size of your thumb, measuring 3-3.7 inches long with a wingspan that could cover a standard envelope at 9-10 inches across. Its most striking feature is its unusually long ears that stand out prominently from its small, mouse-like head. This bat has soft, dense fur that ranges from golden-brown to dark brown, and like all bats, it has thin, leathery wing membranes stretched between elongated finger bones. It's one of our smaller New England bats, weighing less than half an ounce.

idTips.label: Ears
idTips.description: Exceptionally long ears that extend noticeably beyond the nose when pressed forward - much longer than other similar-sized bats. The ears feel thin and papery, almost translucent when backlit.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Small and delicate, about the length of your thumb with a 9-10 inch wingspan. Body feels lightweight and fragile compared to other bat species.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Soft, dense fur ranging from golden-brown to dark chocolate brown. The fur has a silky texture and often appears glossy in good light.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Flies with slow, maneuverable flight patterns close to vegetation. Often seen hawking insects around tree canopies and forest edges at dusk.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Roosts in tree cavities, under loose bark, and in buildings. Look for small, dark pellets of guano (bat droppings) that crumble easily when dry.

habitat: Northern Myotis prefer mature forests with plenty of dead and dying trees that provide roosting cavities under loose bark or in hollow trunks. They're commonly found in mixed hardwood-conifer forests, especially those with oak, maple, and pine trees. During summer, they often roost in buildings, barns, and attics, particularly in rural and suburban areas adjacent to forested land.

seasonality.spring: Emerges from hibernation in late April to May. Pregnant females begin seeking warm maternity roosts in buildings or tree cavities.
seasonality.summer: Most active season with females forming maternity colonies. Young are born in June-July, and you'll see increased evening flight activity as mothers hunt to support nursing.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs in late summer/early fall. Bats begin accumulating fat reserves and may be seen more frequently as they prepare for hibernation.
seasonality.winter: Hibernates in caves, mines, or other underground spaces. Occasionally found in building walls or attics where temperatures remain stable but cool.

funFact: A Northern Myotis can eat up to 1,000 mosquito-sized insects per hour during peak feeding, using echolocation calls so high-pitched that most are completely inaudible to human ears - they're essentially flying around in a world of sound we can't even perceive.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Little Brown Bat, but remember 'long ears, long-eared bat' - if the ears extend well beyond the nose when pressed forward, it's a Northern Myotis. Little Brown Bats have proportionally shorter, more rounded ears that barely reach the nose tip.
contextualKnowledge: The Northern Myotis is currently listed as federally threatened due to White-nose Syndrome, a devastating fungal disease affecting hibernating bats. This makes any sightings particularly valuable for conservation efforts, though the species should never be handled without proper permits and training.
compareHints: Among New England's mouse-eared bats, the Northern Myotis stands out with its distinctively long ears - much longer than the Little Brown Bat's modest rounded ears or the Indiana Bat's medium-length ears. The Eastern Small-footed Myotis is noticeably smaller overall with a black facial mask, while the Northern Myotis lacks this distinctive marking and is larger bodied.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the mouse-eared bats in New England, the little brown bat has the glossiest, most reflective fur compared to the Northern Myotis which appears more matte and grayish-brown.
Compared to its mouse-eared bat cousins like the Little Brown Bat and Northern Myotis, the Eastern Small-footed Myotis is noticeably smaller with that unmistakable black face mask.
Among the mouse-eared bats, Indiana bats are most similar to Little Brown Bats but have smaller feet with less toe hair and distinctive pink lips.
